entries.title: Man, 53, shot inside West Englewood home
entries.summary: <p>A man was critically injured after being shot while inside a home in West Englewood Thursday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 53, was at a residence in the 6900 block of South Oakley Avenue he wasn’t authorized to be in at 7:24 p.m. when a 46-year-old man shot him in the chest, police said. He was taken to Christ Medical Center in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody. The circumstances of the shooting are under investigation, police said. </p>

entries.title: The top matchups from the first round of football playoffs
entries.summary: <p><b>Class 5A</b></p><p><b>No. 24 Providence at No. 18 Kankakee</b></p><p><b>1 p.m. Saturday: </b>Kankakee (7-2) has only one loss on the field — 22-14 vs. No. 1 Lincoln-Way East; the Kays had to forfeit a win against Lincoln-Way West for using an ineligible player. Senior Phillip Turner is an electric dual-threat quarterback who has 1,691 total yards and 22 touchdowns with five interceptions. Sophomore Davion White is a playmaker on both sides of the ball. Providence (7-3) has a prolific offense led by running backs Broden Mackert and Brayden McKay along with quarterback Dominic Vita. The Celtics are 2-3 since interim coach Adam Nissen took over when Tyler Plantz was fired. They played eight playoff qualifiers in the regular season, losing to Mount Carmel, Nazareth and St. Ignatius.</p><p><b>Class 8A</b></p><p><b>Barrington at No. 14 Sandburg</b></p><p><b>7 p.m. Friday: </b>Barrington (6-4) has won six in a row after starting 0-4 against Lyons, Lincoln-Way Central, Naperville North and Hersey. Lamar Osterhues is one of the area’s top running backs with 1,282 rushing yards and 12 touchdowns. Sandburg (7-2) is looking for its first playoff win in 16 years. The Eagles can move the ball on the ground with Army recruit Quinn Durkin or through the air with quarterback Sean Ruisz and tight end Lucas Matykiewicz (Northern Illinois).</p><p><b>Class 8A</b></p><p><b>Glenbrook South</b></p><p><b> at No. 19 New Trier</b></p><p><b>6:30 p.m. Friday: </b>This is the teams’ second matchup in three weeks; New Trier won the first 35-28, also at home. Junior quarterback Liam Kearney of Glenbrook South (6-4) had 280 total yards and two passing touchdowns in the earlier loss. New Trier quarterback Jackie Ryder, a Purdue commit, has accounted for 2,006 total yards while playing just 26 quarters as the Trevians (8-1) won six games by 32 or more points. Their only loss was 35-28 to Maine South.</p><p><b>Class 7A</b></p><p><b>St. Laurence at Plainfield South</b></p><p><b>1 p.m. Saturday: </b>A year after reaching the Class 6A semifinals, St. Laurence (4-6) got into this year’s expanded playoff field as a 39th seed and went on the road to beat Belleville East 25-16 last week. Noah Taylor passed for one touchdown and ran for another for the Vikings, who have Illinois-bound linebacker Sean Rice back from an ankle injury. Plainfield South (8-1) won the Southwest Prairie East and lost only to Oswego. Sophomore quarterback Armani Ford has completed 64% of his passes for 2,429 yards and 19 touchdowns with four interceptions for the Cougars, whose last playoff win was in 2010.</p><p><b>Class 6A</b></p><p><b>Joliet Catholic at</b></p><p><b> Wheaton-Warrenville South</b></p><p><b>7 p.m. Friday: </b>Joliet Catholic (6-4) has one of the area’s best two-way players in senior linebacker/running back Derrick Pomatto, who has 82 tackles and 732 rushing yards with 10 touchdowns. The Hilltoppers closed the regular season with losses to Mount Carmel and IC Catholic before beating Bradley-Bourbonnais 44-3 in the opening round last week. Junior quarterback AJ Rogers has passed for more than 2,000 yards for Wheaton-Warrenville South (6-3), whose only loss since mid-September was 27-24 to Batavia.</p>

entries.title: FDA issues alert about Northfield-based Medline beds tied to fire-related deaths and injuries
entries.summary: <p>The U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued an alert about Northfield-based medical supply company Medline’s beds Thursday after two people died and 16 others were seriously injured by the product.</p><p>The FDA issued an <a class="Link" href="https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/medical-device-recalls-and-early-alerts/early-alert-medline-removes-or-corrects-all-medline-brand-beds-and-accessories" target="_blank" ><u>Early Alert warning</u></a> Thursday about Medline beds for patients in home or long-term care — as well as their accessories, such as mattresses, side rails and more — citing a potential fire hazard. Medline issued its own alert earlier this month saying it was removing the product from sale and exiting the market for the beds.</p><p>The beds’ electrical components have the potential to overheat, causing the casing to melt and produce smoke or cause fires, and the related accessories have the potential to entrap or asphyxiate patients, per the alert. As of Oct. 20, the company said it was aware of at least two deaths and 16 injuries related to the products.</p><p>“We believe this action best supports our commitment to product quality and safety for healthcare providers and the patients and communities they serve,” the company said in a statement. “We recognize the impact this decision may have on the healthcare system. Medline is taking actions to support affected customers and healthcare providers and to help minimize disruption while prioritizing patient safety.”</p><p>For current product owners, Medline says they can still be used, but suggests only plugging in the beds to reposition the patient and not to use extension cords to power them.</p><p>Some of the beds may be able to be repaired, according to the alert, though those that aren’t will be eligible for a full refund or replacement.</p><p>Customers can call Medline recall customer service line at 1-800-950-0128 and choose option No. 7 to start the process. Customers can also report any adverse events, such as fires, to the FDA <a class="Link" href="https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/medwatch/index.cfm" target="_blank" ><u>online</u></a>.</p><p>“The FDA is currently reviewing information about this potentially high-risk device issue and will keep the public informed as significant new information becomes available,” the agency said in a statement.</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams fined again for wearing cleats
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams will continue wearing Caddix cleats, and the NFL will keep fining him.</p><p>One week after he was first fined $11,941 for wearing the cleats against the Falcons — specifically, for showing a logo that wasn’t Nike, Adidas or Under Armour on game day — Williams was fined for donning them against the Patriots, a source confirmed. ESPN reported Williams was fined twice as much as he was for initial transgression: $23,882.</p><p>Williams had expected to be fined. He <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/28/bears-quarterback-caleb-williams-caddix-cleats-nfl-fine-keeping-wearing" target="_blank" >said Wednesday</a> he’d continue wearing the cleats, which claim to reduce stress on players’ joints.</p><p>“I’m focused on being able to be out here for the guys,” Williams said. “And if that can give me a small percentage up [as a fine] and it works, then that’s what I’m gonna do.”</p><p>Williams was not fined earlier in the season when he wore all-white Caddix cleats without a prominent logo. About 40 NFL players have worn them in a game. Caddix co-founder Jack Rasmussen told the Sun-Times this week he'd be "happy to cover his fines."</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks lose to Red Wings as 'pretty much everything' goes wrong
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> coach Jeff Blashill struck a relatively positive tone after many of his team's first eight losses this season, sometimes to a surprising degree considering what the games looked like.</p><p>But after the ninth loss — a 4-1 defeat Thursday against the Red Wings that was more lopsided than the score suggested — there was no positive rhetoric to be found.</p><p>"We've had a lot of games throughout this season where we did a lot of good things and maybe beat ourselves with critical mistakes," Blashill said. "Tonight, to me, wasn't that at all. It's a step backwards. Because you just had too many guys that weren't skating, didn't compete hard enough or [didn't have] enough attention to detail."</p><p>The result kept the Hawks winless on the road (0-5) and squandered their hopes of building momentum from what might've been their best team-wide performance Tuesday against the Kings.</p><p>Maybe the Hawks were still bloated from a festive dinner Wednesday that kicked off the team's biennial "dad's trip." Maybe the Red Wings were extra motivated to prove they don't need Dylan Larkin after the latest dramatic twist in his trade-request saga.</p><p>Or maybe the Hawks as currently constructed — and/or as currently coached — have no chance of sustaining success. The answer remains to be seen. But there was plenty of hand-wringing in the locker room.</p><p>"Overall, it was a pretty poor effect," Ian Cole said. "All of us expected to use Tuesday’s game to springboard us into a string of good play. It was pretty unfortunate we did what we did tonight."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Wings goal: Arvidsson pushes in his second of the game. <a href="https://t.co/ESV8Sel9N8">pic.twitter.com/ESV8Sel9N8</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2115986098446897499?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Patrick Kane's son Trick was at Little Caesar's Arena for his dad's strangely emotional welcome back to Detroit — coming less than three years after his extremely emotional, memorable welcome back to Chicago — but Kane followed that up with a poor night on the ice.</p><p>The Wings outshot the Hawks 10-4 and outscored them 2-0 during Kane's five-on-five ice time, and his seventh minor penalty of the season led to the Wings' go-ahead power-play goal early in the third period.</p><p>Kane said "pretty much everything" went wrong and acknowledged he needs to cut down on his penalties.</p><p>"[It] seems like a lot of them are [me] trying to lift a stick and either getting caught in the hands or high-sticking," he said. "I'll be better in that area."</p>

entries.title: Boycott Bears, Sox if you're angry over teams' threats to move
entries.summary: <p>I'm not a fan of professional sports. It's too expensive for a family. The best thing about my divorce was that I never had to endure another football game. That said, I don't understand why fans aren't revolting over the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears’</a> threats to leave Illinois and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/08/justin-ishbia-new-white-sox-stadium-proposal-south-loop-amtrak-railyard-bridgeport-nicole-lee" >Sox</a> toying with moving away from their devoted fan base. Don't pay. Don't go until they stop trying to blackmail everyone.</p><p><i>Gail Gartelos, Bridgeport</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d30000" name="module-d30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Judging progress on the bench </h3><p>As I was filling out my Chicago ballot a few days ago, I reached the long list of judges up for retention. It immediately struck me that out of the listed judges, most of them were women.</p><p>It wasn’t like that when I first voted. In 1976, I could count the number of female Cook County judges on my hand.</p><p>Today as we face the White House’s relentless assault on diversity, equity and inclusion, the U.S. Supreme Court’s torpedoing of affirmative action and the grotesque misogyny of the online right, it may feel that the progress toward gender equality over the last five decades is being washed away. But it isn’t: As that ballot shows, women have gained lasting positions of power in our society that won’t be erased, in spite of current setbacks.</p><p>So it comes as little surprise that it is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/09/feds-appear-to-hide-name-of-government-lawyer-in-new-broadview-six-court-filing" >U.S. District Judge April Perry</a> who has emerged as the chief force holding the Trump administration accountable for its outrageous and murderous assault on Chicago-area immigrants and their supporters in 2025.</p><p>The struggle for equality is never over. But it is important that we not forget the progress that has been made.</p><p><i>John D. Cameron, West Ridge</i></p><h3>Ego-fueled museum modifications </h3><p>I appreciate Sun-Times architecture critic Lee Bey's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/10/22/griffin-msi-defends-criticized-welcome-hall-design" >column</a> clarifying the controversy about the Welcome Hall proposed for the magnificent Griffin Museum of Science and Industry. Whenever I've visited this astonishing museum, the history of Chicago permeates it with inspiration and brings to life Daniel Burnham's "Make no small plans." It stands as a reminder of who we still are.</p><p>There is a modern ego that finds it necessary to inflict itself on this world-class structure, rather than respectfully enhance its beauty. We're sadly seeing this out of control ego in Washington, D.C., with the giant ballroom being built to dwarf the White House and the odd, Arc de Triomphe structure, which will block the classic historical buildings. I hope that our better selves make the choice to enhance our enchanting, stunning museum and not block it.</p><p><i>Jean Scott, Irving Park</i></p><h3>Endangering humans </h3><p>I'm not surprised that Donald Trump is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/10/20/trump-endangered-species-act-illinois-species-at-risk" >gutting</a> the Endangered Species Act, which puts the future of animals, insects and birds at risk. But what can we expect from a man who has also put the human species at risk?</p><p><i>Mike Levey, Deerfield</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Wedding invitation clashes with dream vacation
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm 78, and my husband is 79. This past year, he lost $500,000 through a fraudulent bitcoin site. Fortunately, we have $500,000 left, but I'm so angry about this, you can't imagine — all of my hard-earned savings, gone. I've had a lifelong dream to go to Italy to see all the amazing art and sculptures. I have scoliosis and suffer from chronic pain, but I don't want this or the loss of money to stop me from finally going.</p><p>This summer, a niece on my husband's side got married. She lives in New York, and we live in Nevada, and I didn't want to go for several reasons. I sent $300 and declined. I'm not sure if that was enough money. Now, I feel conflicted about this while making the decision to finally see Italy. No matter what, no one will be OK with this decision, and I truly need help with letting go of anger and guilt so I can just enjoy it without angst. — <i>WEIGHING THE OPTIONS</i></p><p><b>DEAR OPTIONS:</b> It sounds like you are not particularly close to this niece. If you were, I would have advised against skipping the wedding. However, you already sent a generous gift and politely declined the invitation in a timely manner, which is more than many wedding invitees seem able to manage these days.</p><p>As far as I can tell, your conscience should be perfectly clear at this point. You don't owe your husband or his family any more than you've already given, so this is the perfect time to keep planning that dream vacation. I hope you can use the trip to work out some of the resentment you've been holding. If you focus on your own fulfillment for a while, there's a good chance you'll feel less angry upon your return. Buon viaggio!</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> After working for a large corporation for 40 years, my fiancee is now retired. She goes out with several retired men for a monthly breakfast. I think that their spouses should be included because she's the only woman there. She has commented that they flirt with her. Out of respect for me, shouldn't she stop going? — <i>IFFY IN IOWA</i></p><p><b>DEAR IFFY:</b> This has nothing to do with you. The only reason she should stop going is if she is made to feel uncomfortable. A group breakfast once a month isn't a threat to your relationship. Calm down before you start appearing to be insecure and overbearing.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I need help with the right thing to say to a certain member of our book club when I host. She's a 50-year-old woman who, when she comes to my house, drapes her legs and feet all over the furniture. Isn't that "at home" behavior? What would you say? — <i>FUSSY ABOUT THE FURNITURE</i></p><p><b>DEAR FUSSY:</b> I would take the woman aside and tell her privately that when I entertain guests in my home, I prefer they not drape their legs on my furniture and keep their feet on the floor.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: More raw sewage, billions of gallons of it, is pouring into the Chicago River after storms
entries.summary: <p>Joe Gamble knows what to expect when he arrives at work at the Bridgeport Art Center after days of heavy rain.</p><p>“There was raw sewage floating in the creek,” Gamble says after storms in early October. “The wind carried the smell for at least a block or two.”</p><p>The Bridgeport Art Center sits along the South Branch of the Chicago River at a spot known as Bubbly Creek, a small body of water that marks the South Fork of the river and divides Bridgeport and McKinley Park.</p><p>It’s a really disgusting spot after big storms.</p><p>Layers of feces, condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float past and get stuck in the low-lying trees along the shoreline. There are so many condoms that they’ve picked up a nickname: “Chicago whitefish.”</p><p>More and more people have been drawn to the river in recent years for recreation, many of them taking to the water in canoes and kayaks.</p><p>Bubbly Creek appeals particularly to beginner rowers and paddlers because it's calm and easy to navigate. After storms, though, it often stinks so badly that the smell clings to Gamble’s clothes even after he’s left the area.</p><p>“I am sometimes tolerant of smells,” says Gamble, who works at the Chicago Maritime Museum, “but it’s a different level.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a30000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Joe Gamble works near Bubbly Creek. He says after a big storm it can stink so bad that the smell stays on his clothes even after he’s left the area.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p> Anthony Vazquez / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The culprit behind the stench? A sewage pumping station on Racine Avenue south of the Bridgeport Art Center building. The Racine Avenue pumping station has big pumps that help move sewer water — both wastewater and stormwater — to a treatment facility where it's sanitized, then sent on to the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, then the Des Plaines and Illinois rivers and ultimately to the Mississippi River down to the Gulf of Mexico.</p><p>But sometimes the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, the government body that operates the station, says heavy rains mean it needs to dump untreated sewage directly into the river to prevent flooding of homes. </p><p>And it’s a lot of sewage. This year, the Racine station, which is nearly 90 years old, has dumped more than 10 billion gallons of sewage into the river. That's more than it has since 2019. In Chicago, storm water and wastewater go into one big sewer.</p><p>Like what happens at the Racine station on the South Side, the water reclamation district's North Branch pumping station — at Lawrence Avenue and the river on the North Side, on the border of Albany Park and Lincoln Square — has spewed nearly two billion gallons of untreated sewage this year into the North Branch of the Chicago River.</p><p>And all of this is happening despite the billions of dollars in taxpayers' money that has been spent over 50 years on the Deep Tunnel project, the sprawling system of more than 100 miles of underground tunnels and massive reservoirs designed to capture floodwater in the Chicago area and help protect the river and Lake Michigan from pollution. </p><p>The Deep Tunnel is one of the many ways that government officials in Chicago and engineers have tried to adapt a big city that originally was built on a swamp and remains highly prone to flooding to its environment.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-760000" name="html-embed-module-760000"></a><div style="min-height:655px" id="datawrapper-vis-iAwYu"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/iAwYu/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-iAwYu"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/iAwYu/full.png" alt="Tunnels, reservoirs help prevent some flooding (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>But climate change has complicated those efforts. It's contributing to intensifying weather patterns that bring storms that drop rain faster and harder than ever before. That overwhelms our sewers, streets and homes. </p><p>These intense storms can bring us more than 8.5 inches of rain in just 24 hours. </p><p>But Chicago's sewer system, designed decades ago, can handle just two inches of rain before flooding is likely.</p><p>All of that sewage flowing into Bubbly Creek and the North Branch of the river isn’t just gross. It also poses a health risk for people with weak immune systems because of the bacteria and other pathogens the water carries. The contaminated water also can wreak havoc with nature, wiping out fish populations for weeks. That’s bad for the larger ecosystem, something that environmental advocates and government officials have been working over the past three decades to restore.</p><p>Tara Hoffmann, who is executive director of Recovery on Water, a group that has a rowing team for breast-cancer survivors, worries about keeping its members safe in the sometimes-nasty water. Some of the women have compromised immune systems following their cancer treatment. And they are out on the water, rowing, much of the time during warm weather months.</p><p>Hoffmann recalls a particularly bad day on the creek in June, when the women were paddling through excrement.</p><p>“One of the first things you notice," she says, "is fish up at the surface, gasping for air. They’re just desperate to breathe.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fc0000" Racine and North Branch pumping stations are owned by the water reclamation district. Since 2011, the independent government body that's in charge of treating sewage and reducing flooding around Chicago, has operated under a binding agreement with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over federal clean water violations related to the sewage.</p><p>District officials say the more intense storms we're seeing mean that Chicago needs more flood-prevention measures in addition to the Deep Tunnel, like creating green spaces and tapping other strategies in an effort to capture water before it reaches the sewers. The district has designed nearly 300 flood-mitigation projects, many of them still in the planning stages.</p><p>Raw sewage is a clear threat to the river's water quality, says Phil Nicodemus, who's the research director for the organization Urban Rivers, which works to make urban waterways in Chicago into wildlife sanctuaries.</p><p>“It dumps a bunch of nutrients into the water at the same time,” Nicodemus says of the sewage. “That causes a massive oxygen drop, which causes a huge die-off. If that happens enough times throughout the year, you might be talking about a whole summer without much oxygen at all. That creates an enormous problem for wildlife.”</p><p>On a late summer day, Nicodemus travels in a pontoon boat with a team surveying the floating ecosystems near River Park on the North Side, not far from the North Branch pumping station. He steers the boat. Urban River team members jump into the water and collect bug samples. These will be studied to help provide insights on water quality.</p><p>Other experts also are examining the problem of these raw sewage dumps in the river.</p><p>Bubbly Creek, a former longtime dumping area for discarded animal carcasses from the old Union Stockyards, was studied after a large sewage spill in 2023. What research biologist Austin Happel from the Shedd Aquarium found was disturbing.</p><p>The Chicago River provides a home to hundreds of animal species, and the sewage is having a dramatic impact on them, according to Happel. He has found that oxygen levels dropped while nitrogen levels rose significantly. Fish swam off and didn’t return until weeks later.</p><p>“There’s a stark shift in the food chain,” Happel says.</p><p>Oxygen in the water gets depleted. The river’s contaminated water can wipe out fish populations for weeks, experts say.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Deep Tunnel can’t keep up</h3><h3></h3><p>The Deep Tunnel system includes more than 100 miles of massive tunnels hundreds of feet underground. The tunnels — basically giant pipes — range in diameter from under 10 feet to 35 feet. They help storm water flow to two former rock quarries in the south and southwest suburbs that can hold billions of gallons of water.</p><p>Cleaner water was one of the main reasons it was decided in the 1970s to build the Deep Tunnel, formally known as the Tunnel and Reservoir Plan. The Deep Tunnel also is supposed to ease flooding in and around Chicago. The costly flood-control measure has worked to a degree but not entirely. This is why the Chicago area still sees chronic flooding and the Chicago River continues to be tainted by sewage.</p><p>The intensity of the rains we now see are too much for the tunnel and reservoir system to handle as envisioned. It's being overwhelmed.</p><p>This summer, the biggest of the two quarries — the Thornton reservoir in South Holland — became filled with storm water for the first time since it was opened in 2015. That mean it contained nearly eight billion gallons of sewage. And it still hasn’t completely drained.</p><p>To the west of Chicago, the McCook reservoir in Bedford Park has filled up 10 times this year. Since it was opened in December 2017 through last year, that 3.5 billion-gallon reservoir had filled to capacity only five times.</p><p>McCook is now undergoing an expansion. Eventually, it's expected to hold 10 billion gallons of sewage water when it’s completed in 2032. The water reclamation district previously had told the EPA the expansion would be finished three years sooner, in 2029.</p><p>In the race against time and nature, “The efforts aren’t keeping up,” Nicodemus says.</p><p>Margaret Frisbie, executive director of the environmental advocacy group Friends of the River, agrees. As more people turn to the river for recreation, Frisbie says, the problems are being more widely noticed.</p><p>The answer, she says, will rely on a mix of many new and innovative smaller projects, including moves to create more green space across Chicago and to create structures that capture rain water before it gets into the sewers, where it ultimately can overwhelm the current system.</p><p>This year has been a whopper for rain, with more than 37 inches already recorded at O’Hare Airport and more rain forecast this weekend.</p><p>That's a big hurdle, according to Frisbie.</p><p>“I don’t think you can engineer your way out of that,” she says.</p><p><i>This article was produced as part of a project with a health and climate change reporting fellowship through USC Annenberg’s Center for Health Journalism and Center for Climate Journalism and Communication.</i></p><bsp-list-loadmore data-module class="PageListD" data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-reading-time="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-a60000" name="list-a60000"></a><bsp-listcarousel data-column-count=4 data-mobile-carousel="false"> <div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> Soaked </div> </div> </div> <div class="PageListD-items" data-list-loadmore-items> <div class="PageListD-items-item"> <div class="PagePromoB"data-align-top> <div class="PagePromo-media"><a class="Link" aria-label="Flooding in Chicago is getting worse. entries.title: Chicago judge says she was a victim of convicted extortionist who posed as cocaine king Pablo Escobar's son
entries.summary: <p>A Cook County judge who presides over domestic violence cases says she was a victim of a convicted felon who posed as the son of a Colombian drug lord.</p><p>Jeanne Wrenn is among at least three influential women with whom Jawad Fakroune had relationships as he moved through Chicago social circles, befriending power brokers and celebrities including an NBA player, according to court records and interviews.</p><p>Fakroune, 46, was sentenced earlier this year on extortion charges in federal court in Chicago and now awaits sentencing in a separate, tax-fraud case.</p><p>The FBI says Fakroune, a Moroccan national, told acquaintances he's the son of Pablo Escobar, the late "king of cocaine" who led the Medellin cartel.</p><p>Wrenn — whose late uncle also was a judge and whose sister was a chief of staff to former Mayor Rahm Emanuel — hasn’t been named in the court proceedings related to Fakroune.</p><p>But she acknowledges she once had a relationship with Fakroune, telling the Chicago Sun-Times in a brief interview in her courtroom, “I’m a victim."</p><p>She referred any questions to Todd Pugh, her lawyer, who wouldn't say how they met, the nature of her relationship with Fakroune or how she was a victim.</p><p>“Your questions concern the subject matter of that pending federal prosecution,” Pugh says by email, pointing to the Illinois Code of Judicial Conduct, which he says “does not permit Judge Wrenn to answer them.”</p><p>Fakroune won't comment.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Duarte also is a member of the hearing board for the Illinois Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission, which hears misconduct complaints against lawyers and can issue disciplinary sanctions.</p><p>Duarte handled financial transactions for Fakroune that later came under federal scrutiny, including filing his property taxes, court records show.</p><p>Court records say she was a former romantic partner of Fakroune. Rooney, whose father was chief executive officer of Waste Management, dated Fakroune and was at a restaurant table with him when he pulled a gun on his business partner Adolfo Garcia, according to Garcia’s testimony in a trial.</p><p>Duarte and Rooney couldn’t be reached.</p><p>In federal court in Chicago in July, Fakroune was sentenced to prison in an extortion case for threatening to kill Garcia over a debt he was trying to collect.</p><p>Last month, Fakroune pleaded guilty in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/09/03/pablo-escobar-pro-basketball-fraud-pritzker" target="_blank" ><u>separate, tax-fraud case</u></a><u> </u>and is awaiting sentencing Dec. 1.</p><p>He came to Chicago sometime after his release from prison in New York in 2012 and connected with a network of rich and powerful people, including restaurateur Phil Stefani and an unnamed NBA player who was bamboozled by Fakroune, according to federal authorities.</p><p>Fakroune frequented popular Chicago restaurants, including Chicago Cut Steakhouse and Gibson’s, where he rubbed shoulders with the city’s movers and shakers as well as sports and entertainment figures.</p><p>Among them was the NBA player, whom Fakroune was accused of fleecing. Reporters could not confirm his identity. In the summer of 2022, Tri Star Sports & Entertainment — a business management company known for representing members of reality TV’s Kardashian family — wired $2.45 million from the NBA player to a bank account controlled by Duarte, the FBI said in an affidavit for a search warrant.</p><p>Tri Star, which wasn’t accused of any wrongdoing, didn’t respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Authorities said Fakroune falsely promised to invest the player’s money in cannabis and shipping container operations but instead spent it on his own homes in New York and in the Chicago area and on luxury cars and watches.</p><p>Duarte, who was identified only as Individual A in the FBI affidavit, wired $350,000 of the basketball player’s money to an unidentified restaurant and bar owner, $300,000 to a New York real estate developer for a property Fakroune was using and more than $1.2 million for Fakroune to buy a mansion in Lemont, court records show.</p><p>Federal authorities interviewed the player more than two years later, in November 2024 — and say he lied to them.</p><p>Fakroune called himself Angelino Escobar and would tell people he was related to Pablo Escobar, the drug lord killed in a entries.title: Housing mobility programs help low-income renters move on up
entries.summary: <p>In 1985, Gloria Washington was living in a subsidized apartment in Chicago’s Englewood neighborhood. She says it was infested with rats and roaches, and there were always people drinking and doing drugs outside the building.</p><p>“I didn’t want that life for my two little kids,” recalls Washington, now 70.</p><p>She heard from her cousin about the Gautreaux Assisted Housing Program, a court-ordered program meant to address racial segregation in Chicago that helped low-income residents move to lower-crime, higher-income neighborhoods and suburbs.</p><p>When she was offered an apartment in the far northwest suburbs, she immediately said “yes.”</p><p>Washington remembers hearing that she would be moving to Schaumburg. At the time, she had only heard of the village on TV ads for a Schaumburg auto dealership.</p><p>“I said, ‘Why are they moving me to a car dealing place?’ ” Washington says. “But I just went along with the flow. I just wanted to get out of what situation I was in.”</p><p>Soon, she moved into a brand new, three-bedroom apartment with her young daughter and son. Despite loving her new digs, Washington was nervous about the lack of sidewalks. She had no car and no job, lived away from family, and sometimes got racist comments from people while walking places with her children.</p><p>But Washington also had help from the local township to pay bills. She was able to send her young son to daycare at Harper College, free of charge, while she attended classes there. The Pace Suburban Bus’s Dial-A-Ride service also proved an invaluable tool for getting around. She found a job at a factory, got her associate’s degree, and then started working with adults with intellectual disabilities.</p><p>And the schools for her children, Washington says, were top-notch.</p><p>“[My kids] went to a nice high school with kids whose parents are judges and lawyers and doctors,” she says.</p><p>More than 40 years after she moved to Schaumburg, Washington still lives there. She’s now in a one-bedroom apartment just a few miles away from where she raised her kids. Both are grown and successful, living in nearby suburbs, she said.</p><p>Washington is one of thousands of people who moved from high-poverty Chicago neighborhoods to various suburbs and other parts of the city through the Gautreaux program in the 1980s and ’90s. The program originated from a 1966 lawsuit against the Chicago Housing Authority (CHA) and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) in which residents alleged that the government intentionally placed Black families in segregated communities. The courts sided with the residents and ordered agencies to provide housing vouchers so families could move to mixed-income areas, often suburban, predominantly white or racially integrated neighborhoods. The program provided residents with housing search counseling, landlord outreach and other resources.</p><p>Gautreaux is considered the country’s first housing mobility program, with The New York Times calling it a modern-day “underground railroad” for helping low-income Black residents escape segregation in Chicago and move to suburban areas with more jobs, better schools and safer streets. The success of the Gautreaux program — which ended when it reached its court-ordered target of moving 7,100 families — helped spawn new housing mobility experiments throughout the country.</p><p>But today, as the city faces a housing crisis and many low-income voucher holders still live in segregated communities — some under substandard conditions — there is only one mobility program in Illinois. Researchers and housing advocates say while these programs are costly, they are effective in helping families — especially those with young children — rise out of poverty, and that more resources are needed from the federal government.</p><h3><b>40 years of evidence</b></h3><p>For decades, researchers have studied the effects of neighborhoods on families like Gloria Washington’s. Data from the Gautreaux program and subsequent housing mobility experiments throughout the country have consistently shown that residents moving from high-poverty, high-crime areas to lower-poverty, lower-crime neighborhoods — often referred to as “opportunity areas” — yield positive impacts on metrics like improved mental health and children’s outcomes.</p><p>“We have now almost 40 years of evidence that converges on this fact: It’s not only the family that a child is born into, but the neighborhood she grows up in that shapes her economic fortunes over time,” said Stefanie DeLuca, a professor at Johns Hopkins University and a researcher at <a class="Link" href="https://opportunityinsights.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Opportunity Insights</u></a>, a nonpartisan think tank focused on economic mobility.</p><p>DeLuca has studied housing vouchers and residential mobility for decades.</p><p>“We can’t expect any one policy to do everything, but it’s remarkable what this policy is capable of,” she says.</p><p>In Chicago, about 40,000 households have CHA housing choice vouchers with which they rent apartments from private landlords. Most of those voucher holders live in majority-Black neighborhoods on the city’s South and West sides, according to data from CHA. This has been the case for <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/chicago/2019/05/02/more-section-8-vouchers-in-chicagos-black-neighborhoods-than-a-decade-ago" target="_blank" ><u>decades</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-b00000" name="html-embed-module-b00000"></a><div class="cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper"> <div class="cpm-gfx-embed"> <div style="min-height:513px" id="datawrapper-vis-pUJR5"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/pUJR5/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-pUJR5"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/pUJR5/full.png" alt="Choropleth map" /></noscript></div> </div> <div class="cpm-gfx-embed"> <div style="min-height:513px" id="datawrapper-vis-JAKGc"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/JAKGc/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-JAKGc"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/JAKGc/full.png" alt="Choropleth map" /></noscript></div> </div> </div> <style> .cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper { align-items: start; display: flex; flex-direction: row; gap: 2rem; } .cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper .cpm-gfx-embed { flex: auto; min-width: 18rem; } @media screen and (max-width: 30rem) { .cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper { align-items: stretch; flex-direction: column; gap: 0; } } </style> </div> </div><p>Furthermore, many end up having to return their vouchers because they cannot secure a home in the time frame they are given due to the shortage of affordable housing, credit checks, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/data/2025/05/14/section-8-renters-say-landlords-routinely-reject-their-housing-choice-vouchers" target="_blank" ><u>discrimination</u></a> from landlords based on source of income, DeLuca said.</p><p>That’s where mobility programs — if designed and implemented well — can help by “boosting the power of the voucher,” she said. While mobility is not the solution to poverty in disinvested parts of the city, they serve as a tool to ease low-income residents’ access to better neighborhoods they otherwise may not have been able to, she said.</p><p>DeLuca said the most successful mobility programs are high-touch and sensitive to families throughout the process. They provide support for the housing search and for conversations with landlords, help with paperwork, as well as funds for security deposits and application fees. Some programs do regular check-ins with participants and connect them to social services and support networks in their new neighborhoods.</p><p>“How the vouchers are administered and who the staff are administering them is vitally important because families need emotional support and they need some customized assistance,” she said.</p><p>After she moved to Schaumburg, Gloria Washington had regular meetings with the administrators of the court-mandated Gautreaux program — the Leadership Council for Metropolitan Open Communities. They connected her with Palatine Township, which provided help with bills and pointed her to resources like food pantries and clothing banks. They also gave her a list of nearby churches that donated cars and other items.</p><p>“They didn't throw us out there,” Washington said. “They gave us a list, [and said,] ‘Contact them, tell them what you need.’ ”</p><h3><b>One housing mobility program in the state </b></h3><p>Due to the success stories from Gautreaux, housing mobility programs saw a wave of expansion during the 1990s and 2000s. According to a report by the Poverty & Race Research Action Council, there are about 40 programs throughout the U.S., many of them clustered in the Northeast, New York state, in particular.</p><p>Even as recently as 2016, the Housing Authority of Cook County (HACC) established a Community Choice Program, “designed to help [voucher holders] transition out of racially and ethnically segregated areas of poverty and relocate into suburban Cook County ‘Areas of Opportunity.’ ” HACC discontinued the program in 2023 due to a lack of funds, according to a spokesperson.</p><p>Today, the only housing voucher mobility program in Illinois is through the <a class="Link" href="https://www.thecha.org/resident-programs-services/mobility-counseling-services-program" target="_blank" ><u>CHA</u></a>, and it moves about 200 to 400 families to higher-income, lower-crime Chicago neighborhoods each year. Applicants must be current housing voucher holders who currently don’t live in a mobility area and have dependents up to age 16.</p><p>Julie Brown, the lead counsel for the residents in the Gautreaux case, says mobility programs are considered boutique programs for which there is no dedicated funding from the federal government.</p><p>“There’s no money for mobility programs unless a housing authority figures out a way to find money because mobility is expensive,” she said. “It requires counselors. It requires [paying] higher rents, help with security deposits.”</p><p>Amid shrinking funds from the federal government for safety net programs, Brown said there’s a debate in the housing community: “Is it better to just provide as many vouchers as possible because we have a housing crisis, or is it better to take some of the vouchers and turn them into mobility money to help people move to mobility areas?”</p><p>She added that there needs to be the political will to do both. One <a class="Link" href="https://nlihc.org/resource/bipartisan-family-stability-and-opportunity-vouchers-act-reintroduced-senate-1" target="_blank" ><u>bipartisan bill</u></a> introduced in Congress this fall proposes the addition of 250,000 “housing mobility vouchers” for low-income families with young children.</p><p>Since CHA began tracking data in 2012, its Mobility Counseling Services Program has moved close to 5,000 families to opportunity areas, according to officials.</p><p>Catherine Johnson is executive director of Housing Choice Partners, which runs CHA’s mobility program. She was previously a housing counselor for the Gautreaux program. She says her organization matches voucher holders with Chicago Community Areas that have less than 20% poverty rate and below-median crime rates. Using those parameters, 42 of Chicago’s 77 community areas — from Albany Park and Ashburn to West Lawn and West Town — are considered “mobility areas.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-ff0000" name="html-embed-module-ff0000"></a><div style="min-height:571px" id="datawrapper-vis-IxDfw"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/IxDfw/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-IxDfw"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/IxDfw/full.png" alt="Voucher holders by community area (Choropleth map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Unlike the Gautreaux program, which opened resource-rich suburbs up to families, CHA’s mobility program works within the city’s boundaries.</p><p>Some experts say this makes it harder for families to see the gains that families like Gloria Washington’s saw in the suburbs, with its higher-performing schools and increased resources. They say <a class="Link" href="https://dionissialiprantis.com/pdfs/BRHP_success.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>successful mobility programs</u></a> in places like Baltimore and Seattle take a more regional approach.</p><p>But CHA says many families prefer to stay in the city, and that due to school choice, “families have access to high performing or specialized schools regardless of where they live.”</p><p>Furthermore, Johnson said participants seek mobility moves for various reasons — not just better economic outcomes for their children: Some want to live in safer neighborhoods, others want more amenities near their homes. Johnson also said there are varying reasons for choosing certain neighborhoods over others: staying close to family and other support systems, fear of racial prejudice in areas with few Black residents, proximity to a job. She also added that some families try out their new neighborhoods for a year and move back.</p><p>In the end, the goal is to provide participants with the best options so they can make their own choices for their families, Johnson said.</p><p>“We get a lot of praise … about how the program has helped them to make a move that they would not otherwise have made,” she said. “It has proven to be the answer for many, and it has proven to be what many families needed to help them to get to the next level.”</p><h3><b>‘Better for my kids’</b></h3><p>Crystal Glover knows firsthand what that feels like. After a bout of homelessness following a domestic dispute with her ex-partner that left second-degree burns on her face, the 30-year-old struggled for nearly a year to find an apartment with her housing voucher.</p><p>“I was going on apartments.com and Zillow and all that,” Glover said. “It’s just hard, and there’s so much scamming going on, so many application fees.”</p><div entries.title: Joliet Prison's Fire Alarms Still Broken Despite Deaths
entries.summary: <p>After years of pleading for help, employees at an Illinois mental health prison plagued by deadly fires said that the state made important safety changes following an investigation by <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/public-safety/2026/07/24/joliet-prison-fires-mental-health-illinois-department-corrections" target="_blank" >the Marshall Project, WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times</a> that detailed 70 fires and two deaths there. But the changes don’t go far enough to ensure workers can prevent and adequately respond to frequent fire emergencies, a union for prison employees said.</p><p>Earlier this year, the state Department of Corrections terminated four guards connected to a 2024 fire that led to the death of Jason Stephens, who was incarcerated at Joliet. The department and the guards’ union would not comment on the terminations, which came months after The Marshall Project and Stephens’ family each sued for video footage related to his death.</p><p>AFSCME Council 31, the union representing front-line workers at the Joliet Treatment Center, said that since the investigation of the prison was published in July, the facility has begun to provide more robust fire safety training, fire-retardant mattresses and full oxygen tanks for employees in case of fires. But they said the prison still has not provided workers with a written fire safety plan. And for the fourth year in a row, an annual inspection by the Office of the State Fire Marshal showed that the prison’s alarms remain broken.</p><p>“Everybody's risking their lives when we have these fires. So it is very important that they get a safety plan so we can all learn what to do,” said Sheena McClain, a corrections treatment officer at the Joliet Treatment Center and local union president.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Corrections did not respond to questions about why fire alarms remain broken after the news organizations’ investigation. A spokesperson for the governor's office said the department is working with the fire marshal to make changes “with great urgency.” The governor's office declined to offer details, citing pending litigation.</p><p>The Joliet Treatment Center was designed to help people with serious mental illness. But men there said they were so desperate for therapy, medical care and time out of their cells that they set their belongings — or themselves — on fire to get attention.</p><p>Following the investigation, Illinois lawmakers called for changes and scheduled two hearings for Nov. 10 related to mental healthcare, conditions at Joliet Treatment and prison oversight.</p><p>In the months leading up to his death in the summer of 2024, Stephens repeatedly complained the prison was failing to treat his sickle cell disease, causing him extreme pain. He threatened to continue harming himself until they gave him help. Then he set his cell on fire.</p><p>Guards left him locked in the smoke-filled cell for around 30 minutes, according to surveillance video reviewed by The Marshall Project. Then, when the fire department put him in an ambulance to go to the hospital, guards would not open the gate for almost 28 more minutes because they were waiting on paperwork and guards to accompany the ambulance.</p><p>Stephens died two weeks later.</p><p>The employees who were fired included an officer who arrived at Stephen's cell during the fire and another who was at the gate when the ambulance attempted to leave. None of the employees could be reached for comment.</p><p>Terah Tollner, a lawyer for Stephens’ estate, said that she doesn’t think it’s a coincidence that the facility didn’t fire any officers until after his family filed a lawsuit and obtained video of the incident. The family said it wants more comprehensive mental health treatment and fire safety plans at the Joliet Treatment Center, so that similar tragedies don’t happen again. Stephens’ estate has filed a separate lawsuit over his death; that remains ongoing.</p><p>Since the news organizations’ investigation, some men incarcerated at the facility said they had seen improvements to mental health care, including better access to a psychiatrist. But they also said that services like one-on-one therapy remain rare.“You can lose yourself in jail,” one incarcerated man said. “This place is for treatment. But people come here, and they don't get better. They deteriorate."</p><p>Illinois State Rep. Lindsey LaPointe, a Chicago Democrat, said she hopes the upcoming hearings will create urgency around the issue of mental health treatment in the state’s prisons.</p><p>“We expect the hearing to pull back the curtain on what the state says it provides vs. what it actually provides,” she said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/public-safety/2026/07/24/joliet-prison-fires-mental-health-illinois-department-corrections" target="_blank" >At Joliet prison, desperate men set themselves on fire</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.themarshallproject.org/2026/08/11/illinois-joliet-deadly-prison-fires-findings" target="_blank" >Why did an Illinois prison fail to stop 70 fires?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/public-safety/2026/08/04/illinois-lawmakers-decry-prisons-gut-wrenching-heartbreaking-conditions" target="_blank" >Illinois lawmakers decry prison’s ‘gut-wrenching,’ ‘heartbreaking’ conditions</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.summary: <p>Hall of Fame linebacker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/06/its-official-bears-legend-brian-urlacher-certifies-qb-caleb-williams-as-badass-says-hes-here-to-stay" >Brian Urlacher</a> will join ESPN’s Manningcast alternate broadcast of the Bears-Seahawks game Monday. That Bears team lost to Peyton Manning and the Colts in Super Bowl XLI.</p><p>He is their all-time leader with 1,361 tackles, ranks 11th with 41 1/2 sacks and is 11th with 22 interceptions.</p><p>The game will air on ESPN nationally and WCIU locally, and the Manningcast is available on ESPN2 and the ESPN app.</p><p>The network did not have a Manningcast for the Bears-Eagles “Monday Night Football” game last month.</p><p>The Manningcast had actor Bill Murray for their broadcast of the 2025 season opener between the Bears and Vikings and former president Barack Obama for a 2022 Bears game against the Patriots.</p>

entries.title: Vocalo brewed up this year's witchiest Halloween playlist. Press play and start the party
entries.summary: <p>What’s scarier than your Halloween costumes? Trying to make sure everyone is enjoying the music at your costume party. If you’re at a loss for a playlist, look no further.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-c00000" name="html-embed-module-c00000"></a><iframe data-testid="embed-iframe" style="border-radius:12px" src="https://open.spotify.com/embed/playlist/6wNVb9tKBoHN58qVnkzpnj?utm_source=generator&si=54a4826a5acd4a17" width="100%" height="352" frameBorder="0" allowfullscreen="" allow="autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; fullscreen; picture-in-picture" loading="lazy"></iframe> </div> </div><p>The Vocalo team — plus some colleagues at WBEZ and the Sun-Times — put together two-plus hours of music, with no “Monster Mash,” “Ghostbusters,” “Time Warp” or “Thriller” in sight. Dance along to less overplayed on-theme songs like “Vamp Anthem” by Playboi Carti, “Dracula” by Tame Impala and “Witchy” by KAYTRANADA and Childish Gambino.</p><p>Give some love to other classics including Warren Zevon’s “Werewolves of London,” “Psycho Killer” by the Talking Heads and Ministry’s “Every Day Is Halloween.” Plus, check out horror film originals like 21 Savage’s “Spiral,” unofficially Halloween songs like “Heads Will Roll” by the Yeah Yeah Yeahs and others that just sound like the soundtrack to a themed party, like Nelly Furtado’s “Maneater.”</p><p>Hit play while you’re getting your costume on, in the car on the way to your Halloween plans or when your friend puts you on music duty at the party.</p>

entries.title: Vatican confirms Pope Leo voted in midterm election, submitted mail ballot in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The Vatican on Friday confirmed that Pope Leo has submitted his mail ballot in Chicago, making him the first pontiff in history to vote in a U.S. election. </p><p>"Pope Leo XIV has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so. The Holy See Press Office confirms that in keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago," the Vatican said in a statement on Friday. </p><p>The Vatican also confirmed that the pope "exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so," including when he lived in Peru. </p><p>"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the statement says.</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times on Thursday reported that Chicago-born Pope Leo is still a registered voter in Illinois and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/10/29/pope-leo-xiv-mail-ballot-illinois-midterm-election" target="_blank" >requested a mail ballot for the midterm elections</a> on Oct. 3 through the Will County clerk's office. </p><p>“Robert Francis Prevost is on the list of individuals who requested a vote by mail ballot for the upcoming election,” Kim Fladhammer, Will County clerk’s office chief of staff, told the Sun-Times. </p><p>Records show Prevost voted in the 2012, 2014 and 2016 Republican primaries, as well as in the 2012, 2014, 2018 and 2024 general elections. He also voted in Democratic primaries in 2008 and 2010. He did not vote in Illinois’ March primary. In Illinois, voters do not have to register by party and can choose parties for their primary ballot. </p><p>The pope has now weighed in on the U.S. Senate race to replace Sen. Dick Durbin and Gov. JB Pritzker’s reelection bid, as well as Will County judicial and county races, among other races.</p><p>The Illinois State Board of Elections on Thursday said any Illinois registered voter can vote by mail and U.S. citizens who are overseas have the right to do so with a law called UOCAVA, The Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act.</p><p>Pritzker made note of the pope voting on social media on Thursday, writing, "If the Pope can vote all the way from Vatican City, you can too!" </p>

entries.title: Miembro de la junta escolar fue suspendido de escuela chárter tras comportamiento no deseado con colega, según registros
entries.summary: <p>Un candidato que busca la reelección en una reñida contienda por la junta escolar de Chicago fue suspendido de su trabajo en una escuela chárter en 2018 después de que una investigación del operador de la escuela concluyó que se embriagó en un evento de trabajo y actuó de forma inapropiada con una compañera, según una carta obtenida por el Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>La carta, enviada a Carlos Rivas Jr. por la Noble Network of Charter Schools en septiembre de 2018, dice que una investigación interna determinó que Rivas incurrió en “contacto físico no deseado con otro empleado sin consentimiento” en violación de la política de Noble contra el acoso durante un evento en el hotel The Robey Chicago en agosto de 2018.</p><p>Según la carta, Rivas estaba intoxicado “hasta el punto de que, por su propia admisión”, no pudo negar las acusaciones debido a “una incapacidad para recordar” lo ocurrido esa noche. En ese momento, Rivas era gerente de apoyo a exalumnos y asuntos externos en UIC College Prep.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7c0000" name="module-7c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La investigación de 2018 y sus conclusiones vuelven a salir a la luz a menos de una semana de que los votantes acudan a las urnas el 3 de noviembre y <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/10/29/lo-que-necesitas-saber-sobre-la-historica-eleccion-de-la-junta-de-educacion-de-chicago" target="_blank" >elijan a todos los 21 miembros de la junta escolar</a> por primera vez.</p><p>Rivas, que representa al distrito 3b del lado noroeste, intenta defenderse del aspirante Jason Dónes, quien cuenta con el respaldo del Sindicato de Maestros de Chicago (CTU). Our Schools, un comité de acción política (PAC) financiado por el CTU, está distribuyendo folletos que destacan la investigación y exhortan a los votantes a oponerse a Rivas. El grupo ha gastado alrededor de $20,000 en apoyo a la candidatura de Dónes hasta finales de septiembre.</p><p>Rivas dijo que fue “decepcionante” ver que el asunto resurgiera tan cerca de la elección.</p><p>“Esto fue hace ocho años, durante un periodo increíblemente difícil mientras cuidaba a mi madre, que padecía insuficiencia renal terminal y demencia”, dijo Rivas en un comunicado. “Acepté la responsabilidad, recibí apoyo a través del programa de asistencia al empleado de Noble, y seguí sirviendo a estudiantes y familias en Noble durante cuatro años más.</p><p>“Esa experiencia forma parte de por qué he impulsado el apoyo en salud mental para los empleados escolares en la junta de educación”, continuó Rivas. “Creo en la rendición de cuentas, el crecimiento y las segundas oportunidades. Estoy orgulloso de mi trayectoria y sigo concentrado en los estudiantes y las familias del Distrito 3b”.</p><p>Según la carta de 2018, Noble ya le había advertido previamente a Rivas sobre embriagarse en eventos relacionados con el trabajo.</p><p>Rivas aceptó estipulaciones como “una última oportunidad” para continuar en la escuela chárter, indica la carta. Eso incluía una suspensión de 10 días sin goce de sueldo, abstenerse de “sustancias intoxicantes” mientras estuviera trabajando o en eventos relacionados con el trabajo y buscar consejería a través del programa de asistencia al empleado del operador chárter.</p><p>“El incumplimiento de los términos de este acuerdo, la falta de mejoría o la recurrencia de cualquier conducta inapropiada dará lugar al despido inmediato”, señala la carta.</p><p>Rivas mantuvo su puesto en Noble hasta 2022, cuando se convirtió en director de asuntos públicos de la Oficina Civil de Responsabilidad Policial (COPA), cargo que todavía ocupa. Noble no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentario.</p><p>Rivas se postuló para la junta escolar en 2024, donde también se enfrentó a Dónes, y ganó con el 54% de los votos. Durante su tiempo en la junta, Rivas ha adoptado un enfoque fiscalmente conservador con el presupuesto escolar. Fue uno de los seis miembros de la junta escolar que votó en contra de aprobar un presupuesto que incluía ingresos no comprometidos del estado.</p><p>En la elección de este año, Rivas cuenta con el apoyo del Consejo Estatal de Illinois del Sindicato Internacional de Empleados de Servicio (SEIU), que representa a miles de empleados de mantenimiento y apoyo de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS). También cuenta con el respaldo del Common Ground Collective, un PAC fuertemente financiado por el multimillonario Michael Sacks y que ha adoptado posturas opuestas a las del CTU.</p><p>Ambos hombres crecieron en Humboldt Park y se identifican como progresistas.</p><p>Las escuelas del distrito 3b enfrentan escasez de maestros y consejeros, aumentos en los impuestos a la propiedad y baja matrícula en medio de una rápida gentrificación y cambios en el vecindario.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Ariel Parrella-Aureli de Block Club Chicago </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: 2016 Cubs roundtable: World Series stars take fresh look back at just how good team really was
entries.summary: <p>Dexter Fowler can’t believe how long it has been since the “Welcome to the team!” texts poured in before the 2016 season.</p><p>They came from Manny Machado, Adam Jones, Ubaldo Jimenez and others — all members of the Orioles — after some erroneous reporting in the media. A couple of days later, the free-agent outfielder re-signed with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> and then hid in a car for 15 minutes at the team’s spring training complex before strolling onto the field and surprising his stunned pals.</p><p>“One of the happiest moments of my life, the love I felt,” the former leadoff hitter says now.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/chicago-cubs-world-series-2016-team-story-10-years-later" target="_blank" >curse-busting World Series championship awaited all of them</a>, the memories made along the way of the sort that last forever.</p><p>Game 7 starter Kyle Hendricks still laughs at himself for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/04/12/kyle-kendricks-cubs-angels-2016-world-series-cleveland-nlcs-dodgers-joe-maddon" target="_blank" >following Jon Lester and John Lackey around like a lost puppy</a> and treasures the way Jake Arrieta looked out for him. Game 6 winner Arrieta still misses dinners on the road that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/22/2016-cubs-great-jake-arrieta-reflects-on-unforgettable-run-on-top-of-the-pitching-world" target="_blank" >never felt quite the same on any other team</a>. Series MVP Ben Zobrist still can’t forget — or stop howling about — the sight of first baseman Anthony Rizzo’s bare behind as he stood with his arms in the air like Rocky Balboa and fired up the clubhouse before Games 5, 6 and 7 against the Guardians.</p><p>Nothing beats those old stories, if — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/chicago-cubs-world-series-2016-team-story-10-years-later" target="_blank" >almost exactly 10 years since the Cubs stormed the mound in Cleveland</a> — we can call them “old.”</p><p>But how do the Cubs reflect on what happened on the field? We discussed that with Arrieta, Fowler, Hendricks, Zobrist, staff ace Lester and the reliever who got the last out in Game 7, Mike Montgomery. Here’s some of what they said, lightly edited for clarity:</p><h3><b>Were the 2016 Cubs the best team you ever played for?</b></h3><p><b>Fowler: </b>“Yes, 100%. Just on paper, really, really good. Also in the locker room, everybody was always together. Those are brothers and always will be brothers for life.”</p><p><b>Zobrist: </b>“It’s hard to say the best; it depends who the opposition is. If we were facing a real power pitching team, I think the 2015 Royals would’ve been the best; we were tough to strike out. But if you put that Cubs offense against the Royals, it’s going to be a fight because the Cubs hit some bombs. Neck and neck, just different in regard to how we won games.”</p><p><b>Lester: </b>“I think talent-wise, the 2007 Red Sox were probably the best team I’ve ever seen on the field. Depth in the lineup, in the rotation, in the bullpen, a lockdown closer; it was pretty impressive. And then I would probably put the 2013 Red Sox and the 2016 Cubs as a little bit of a tie. I think ’16 had more talent than ’13, but as far as just fun and the best groups I’ve been around, I would put them as a tie. In ’13 we had a bunch of rejects on one-year deals, end of careers, supposedly in a rebuild, but got a bunch of lunatics together and said, ‘Hey, that sounds good’ and then went and won.”</p><p><b>Hendricks: </b>“Yes, for sure — in so many different ways. Best team I’ve ever played for, best guys I’ve ever played with, best coaching, best players, best everything.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/chicago-cubs-world-series-2016-team-story-10-years-later" target="_blank" >10 years after: How Cubs went from lovable losers to 2016 World Series champions</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><h3><b>Where do those Cubs belong in the pecking order of World Series champions?</b></h3><p><b>Arrieta: </b>“In terms of where we stack up talent-wise, probably not at the top, but it’s not always about that. It’s about coming through in the most pivotal of moments. Also, I think what made us so good was the personalities and the character behind that team. Relationships and lifelong friendships are what made us so special. If we don’t have those bonds, we don’t perform the same way on the field, I guarantee that.”</p><p><b>Hendricks: </b>“In a single-season setting, we were a great team. It’s hard to put that in the scope of baseball, though. Our focus was so solely around the city of Chicago, the 108 years. We wanted to be the greatest team for Chicago in the context of history.”</p><p><b>Lester: </b>“This is a very politically correct answer, but I feel like anybody who ever won a championship ought to be tied for first. The way we figured out how to pull the rope at the same time, that was rare.”</p><p><b>Zobrist: </b>“I would put that team up against any team in history as far as the clutch ability to come back from the brink in the midst of the most pressure any team has faced.”</p><p><b>Fowler: </b>“We were stacked — no holes. Our pitching staff, our lineup, Cy Youngs and All-Stars up and down, it was crazy. We had seven All-Stars that year, and five of us were starters. You play us seven games against any of these Dodgers teams, we’re winning at least four of those.”</p><p><b>Montgomery: </b>“I would say it was one of the top three to five championship runs by a team in baseball ever solely due to the ‘curse.’ But also there were all the personalities. Someone like me as an unsung hero? The David Ross situation in Game 7? I don’t think it’s about who was better, though. You’ll never know, and it’s a dead-end argument.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Xl3iZpcAb2g?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Chicago Cubs World Series Highlights 2016!"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Who was the best — or most important — player on that Cubs team?</b></h3><p><b>Fowler: </b>“Most important and best is totally different to me. On paper, Kris Bryant was the best player. But most important? It’s a toss-up. We had some pitchers, man.”</p><p><b>Arrieta: </b>“That’s very hard to answer. Jason Heyward’s leadership and selflessness, there’s an MVP in that. Anthony Rizzo’s and David Ross’ vocal leadership were priceless. The way Jon Lester led by example was, too. Same with Dexter with his smile and charisma and energy. I can’t pick one.”</p><p><b>Zobrist: </b>“Rizzo and Bryant, from a position-player standpoint, were irreplaceable. KB was the MVP of the league; how he played defense and ran the bases gave the other team so much to think about. Together, that tandem, they made pitchers have to work so hard that by the time they got to me, if I was batting cleanup, they were too tired to focus on me. We needed those two to come through, and they did. Those two were the backbone of our lineup.”</p><h3><b>Are you surprised those Cubs never made it back to a World Series?</b></h3><p><b>Lester: </b>“It’s a little surprising, but baseball’s hard. In 2017, we still had a great team and we competed, but we may have run out of some steam. I think the guys that were in it understand how hard it is to do it again. Look at the teams spending more money than everybody else. You have to go out and spend that kind of money year in and year out to get the pieces you need. But I am surprised we didn’t at least get back into another one.”</p><p><b>Hendricks: </b>“I think the expectation was you get there and go back to the playoffs and ‘This is how it happens.’ You don’t realize how hard it is at the time. It always leaves you wanting more, wanting that feeling again. Our group remained so special, but, yeah, it was disappointing.”</p><p><b>Montgomery: </b>“Deep down, I thought we had the team for three to five years where we should’ve won multiple World Series. There was always a feeling of, ‘What if?’ It just makes me appreciate that ’16 team even more.”</p><p><b>Fowler: </b>“I think if we all stayed together — all of us — we would’ve won multiple.”</p><p><b>Zobrist: </b>“I knew 2017 was going to be an uphill climb; everybody was exhausted at the beginning. I was more disappointed in 2018 and 2019. I really thought we had a chance both years. I was surprised we didn’t get there. entries.title: Boo, who? College football's Halloween Saturday promises more October spookiness
entries.summary: <p>A Week 9 Halloween Saturday in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >college football</a>?</p><p>It’s rather anticlimactic, at least in terms of boos and frights.</p><p>That’s because the top teams in the country already spent much of October holding on to the walls in a desperate attempt — failing, in many cases — to make it through a haunted house of a month without soiling themselves.</p><p>In Week 6, No. 1 Texas lost to unranked Oklahoma, LSU lost to unranked Kentucky and popular national championship pick Oregon lost at home to unranked UCLA.</p><p>In Week 7, No. 1 Georgia lost at home to unranked Auburn, Texas lost at home to unranked Florida and three other presumed title contenders — Notre Dame, Indiana and Alabama — went down.</p><p>And in Week 8, No. 2 BYU fell at unranked UCF while Texas Tech, Tennessee, Iowa and USC all took it on the chin from unranked foes.</p><p>The “unranked” thing has become one of the dominant themes of a season in which upsets — otherwise known as bad losses — have been the norm and only three unbeaten teams remain, well below what’s usually the case as November nears. Does anybody out there really think No. 1 Miami, No. 9 UCLA and No. 10 Utah will avoid getting dinged eventually? Put me down for a “no” on all three.</p><p>It boggles the mind to think about the College Football Playoff committee eventually managing to seed the 12-team tournament to anyone’s satisfaction. The disagreement — speaking of boos — might be louder and lustier than ever.</p><p>Meanwhile, the “unranked” thing has seeped all the way into my addled brain as I consider my predictions for this weekend’s games. A trick or a treat? Heck, I don’t know. Just take the Milk Duds and get off my stoop.</p><h3><b>Week 9 picks</b></h3><p><i>All games Saturday; my picks to cover listed first.</i></p><p><b>Illinois (-2½) at Maryland </b>(11 a.m., FS1, 890-AM): Playing in place of injured quarterback Katin Houser, Michael Clayton last week became only the third Illini true freshman ever to win a start, a 21-10 upset of Oregon. Clayton threw for only 84 yards in that game, though, which won’t cut it on the road — not even against the dysfunctional Terrapins, who are down a head coach after Mike Locksley was fired. pouring into the Chicago River after storms </a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddyoil-l-h/" target="_blank" >Brett Chase</a></h5><p><b>Smell test</b>: After heavy rain, Chicagoans near Bubbly Creek have come to expect putrid smells from the small body of water that marks the South Fork of the Chicago River and divides Bridgeport and McKinley Park. The odor is from raw sewage in the creek. Layers of feces, condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float past and get stuck in the low-lying trees along the shoreline.</p><p><b>Why is this happening?</b>: In Chicago, stormwater and wastewater go into one big sewer. That water should run through a sewage pumping station and be moved to a treatment facility. But sometimes the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago dumps untreated sewage directly into the river to prevent flooding of homes.</p><p><b>The scale</b>: This year, the sewage pumping station on Racine Avenue near Bridgeport has dumped more than 10 billion gallons of sewage into the river. The North Branch pumping station, on the border of Albany Park and Lincoln Square, has spewed nearly two billion gallons of untreated sewage into the North Branch of the Chicago River this year.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: Climate change is contributing to intensifying weather patterns that bring storms that drop rain faster and harder than ever before. The intense rain overwhelms our sewers, streets and homes. Chicago's sewer system can handle just two inches of rain before flooding is likely. All of that sewage flowing into Bubbly Creek and the North Branch of the river threatens wildlife and poses health risks for people with weak immune systems.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddyoil-l-k/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>LET’S DISCUSS 🌧️</h4><p>We're hosting a community dinner and discussion about why flooding is getting worse in Chicago on Thursday, Nov. 12 at the Garfield Park Field House.</p><p>Have you experienced flooding?
